{"problem": {"theorem": "Prove that any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "abstract_algebra", "proof_text": "\begin{proof}

    By Cauchy's theorem we have that if $G$ is a group of order 21 then it has an element $a$ of order 3 and an element $b$ of order 7. We know $i \neq$ 0 since that implies $a b=a$ and so that $b=e$, a contradiction, and we know $i \neq 1$ since then $a b=b a$ and this would imply $G$ is abelian, which we are assuming is not the case.

Now, $a$ has order 3 so we must have $b=a^3 b a^{-3}=b^{i^3}$ mod 7 , and so $i$ is restricted by the modular equation $i^3 \equiv 1 \bmod 7$

\begin{center}

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|}

\hline$x$ & $x^3 \bmod 7$ \\

\hline 2 & 1 \\

\hline 3 & 6 \\

\hline 4 & 1 \\

\hline 5 & 6 \\

\hline 6 & 6 \\

\hline

\end{tabular}

\end{center}

Therefore the only options are $i=2$ and $i=4$. Now suppose $G$ is such that $a b a^{-1}=b^2$ and let $G^{\prime}$ be another group of order 21 with an element $c$ of order 3 and an element $d$ of order 7 such that $c d c^{-1}=d^4$. We now prove that $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic. Define

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi: G & \rightarrow G^{\prime} \\

a & \mapsto c^{-1} \\

b & \mapsto d

\end{aligned}

$$

since $a$ and $c^{-1}$ have the same order and $b$ and $d$ have the same order this is a well defined function. Since

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi(a) \phi(b) \phi(a)^{-1} & =c^{-1} d c \\

& =\left(c d^{-1} c^{-1}\right)^{-1} \\

& =\left(d^{-4}\right)^{-1} \\

& =d^4 \\

& =\left(d^2\right)^2 \\

& =\phi(b)^2

\end{aligned}

$$

$\phi$ is actually a homomorphism. {"kind":"proof","text":"Let \(G\) and \(H\) be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order \(21\). We first establish a common normal form for either group \(K\in\{G,H\}\).

By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups divides \(3\) and is congruent to \(1\pmod 7\), so it is \(1\). Thus the Sylow \(7\)-subgroup \(P=\langle b\rangle\) is normal. Choose a subgroup \(Q=\langle a\rangle\) of order \(3\). Since \(P\cap Q=\{e\}\) and \(|P||Q|=21\), we have \(K=PQ\), and every element of \(K\) has a unique expression \(b^j a^i\), where \(0\le j<7\) and \(0\le i<3\).

Because \(P\) is normal, conjugation by \(a\) induces an automorphism of \(P\), so
\[
aba^{-1}=b^r
\]
for some \(r\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). Since \(a^3=e\),
\[
b=a^3ba^{-3}=b^{r^3},
\]
so \(r^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(r\equiv1,2,4\pmod 7\). If \(r=1\), then \(a\) commutes with \(b\); because \(a,b\) generate \(K\), this would make \(K\) abelian. Hence \(r=2\) or \(r=4\). If \(r=4\), replace \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\); the resulting conjugation exponent is \(4^{-1}\equiv2\pmod 7\). Therefore generators may be chosen so that
\[
a^3=b^7=e,\qquad aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]

Applying this to both groups, choose generators \(a,b\) of \(G\) and \(c,d\) of \(H\) satisfying
\[
aba^{-1}=b^2,\qquad cdc^{-1}=d^2.
\]
Define
\[
\phi:G\to H,\qquad \phi(b^j a^i)=d^j c^i.
\]
The uniqueness of the normal forms makes \(\phi\) well-defined and bijective. Moreover,
\[
(b^j a^i)(b^\ell a^k)=b^{j+2^i\ell}a^{i+k},
\]
and the identical formula holds in \(H\):
\[
(d^j c^i)(d^\ell c^k)=d^{j+2^i\ell}c^{i+k}.
\]
Consequently \(\phi(xy)=\phi(x)\phi(y)\) for all \(x,y\in G\). Thus \(\phi\) is an isomorphism. Since \(G\) and \(H\) were arbitrary, any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic.","reason":"The proof uses Sylow theory to obtain unique normal forms, normalizes the two possible nontrivial conjugation actions, and verifies the isomorphism directly from the multiplication rule."}

{"kind":"proof","text":"Let \(G\) and \(H\) be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order \(21\). We first establish a common normal form for either group \(K\in\{G,H\}\).

By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups divides \(3\) and is congruent to \(1\pmod 7\), so it is \(1\). Thus the Sylow \(7\)-subgroup \(P=\langle b\rangle\) is normal. Choose a subgroup \(Q=\langle a\rangle\) of order \(3\). Since \(P\cap Q=\{e\}\) and \(|P||Q|=21\), we have \(K=PQ\), and every element of \(K\) has a unique expression \(b^j a^i\), where \(0\le j<7\) and \(0\le i<3\).

Because \(P\) is normal, conjugation by \(a\) induces an automorphism of \(P\), so
\[
aba^{-1}=b^r
\]
for some \(r\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). Since \(a^3=e\),
\[
b=a^3ba^{-3}=b^{r^3},
\]
so \(r^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(r\equiv1,2,4\pmod 7\). If \(r=1\), then \(a\) commutes with \(b\); because \(a,b\) generate \(K\), this would make \(K\) abelian. Hence \(r=2\) or \(r=4\). If \(r=4\), replace \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\); the resulting conjugation exponent is \(4^{-1}\equiv2\pmod 7\). Therefore generators may be chosen so that
\[
a^3=b^7=e,\qquad aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]

Applying this to both groups, choose generators \(a,b\) of \(G\) and \(c,d\) of \(H\) satisfying
\[
aba^{-1}=b^2,\qquad cdc^{-1}=d^2.
\]
Define
\[
\phi:G\to H,\qquad \phi(b^j a^i)=d^j c^i.
\]
The uniqueness of the normal forms makes \(\phi\) well-defined and bijective. Moreover,
\[
(b^j a^i)(b^\ell a^k)=b^{j+2^i\ell}a^{i+k},
\]
and the identical formula holds in \(H\):
\[
(d^j c^i)(d^\ell c^k)=d^{j+2^i\ell}c^{i+k}.
\]
Consequently \(\phi(xy)=\phi(x)\phi(y)\) for all \(x,y\in G\). Thus \(\phi\) is an isomorphism. Since \(G\) and \(H\) were arbitrary, any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic.","reason":"The proof uses Sylow theory to obtain unique normal forms, normalizes the two possible nontrivial conjugation actions, and verifies the isomorphism directly from the multiplication rule."}
